abstract.p: Callus formation and differentiation are direct manifestation of plant cell totipotency, tightly regulated by key hormone signals and tissue-specific genes. Carrot (Daucus carota L.) is a widely cultivated vegetable with high economic and nutritional values, for which callus culture serves as the fundamental technique in rapid propagation and functional genomics. However, callus induction and differentiation efficiency vary substantially across carrot genotypes, and the underlying molecular regulatory networks remain poorly characterized. To investigate the molecular regulatory mechanisms governing callus development, a comparative transcriptomic dataset was generated from four Daucus carota lines characterized by distinct callus induction and differentiation capacities. Samples were collected at four time points during the callus culture process to obtain transcriptomic expression datasets. The RNA sequencing data were generated by MGI platform, yielded a total of 399.48 Gb of high-quality data (average 6 Gb per library, Q30 ≥ 97%). This transcriptome dataset serves as a core resource for elucidating the molecular mechanisms of dedifferentiation, stress adaptation, and totipotency in carrot callus, providing insights into plant cell plasticity and supporting comparative genomics and applications in crop regeneration. The raw sequencing data are publicly available in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under the BioProject accession number PRJNA1398431.

list-item.p: This transcriptome dataset provides comprehensive transcriptomic profiles of carrot callus, covering multiple genotypes and developmental stages. It serves as a core resource for researches on plant cell dedifferentiation and redifferentiation, and supports both fundamental and applied studies in plant biology.

This dataset contains transcriptional information related to the transition of plant cells from differentiated state to totipotent callus. It can be used to explore the corresponding transcriptional regulatory network, and provides basic data for studies on plant cell plasticity and developmental reprogramming.

Researchers can use this resource to identify key genes involved in carrot callus formation, analyze the signaling and regulatory pathways controlling dedifferentiation, and compare totipotency-related gene expression patterns between wild and cultivated carrot germplasms.

This dataset is compatible with homologous transcriptomic datasets from model species (e.g., Arabidopsis thaliana, Nicotiana tabacum) for comparative analysis. It enables the exploration of conserved and species-specific regulatory mechanisms in callus development, and provides data support for optimizing regeneration systems in other crops.

This dataset includes transcriptional data of carrot callus under culture conditions, which can be used to mine key genes responsive to oxidative stress and osmotic stress during callus culture, and explore the transcriptional regulatory basis of callus stress adaptation.

sec.title: Background
sec.p:
Callus is a mass of dividing parenchyma cells generated through plant cell dedifferentiation, and serves as essential material for plant in vitro propagation and genetic transformation. Carrot (Daucus carota) is a globally cultivated vegetable valued for its nutrient-rich fleshy root containing carotenoids and dietary fiber [1]. Although callus induction and differentiation systems have been established in multiple crop species, there are significant variations in induction efficiency across different species and even among different germplasms within the same species [2]. Moreover, the molecular regulatory networks underlying this process remain poorly characterized. Most existing studies focus on single genotype, leaving genotype-dependent differences in totipotency in totipotency unexplored. While physiological and molecular mechanisms underlying carrot callus induction and development remain poorly understood [3]. In this study, RNA-seq technology was employed to generate a transcriptome dataset covering multiple carrot genotypes and developmental stages (Fig. 1). This dataset supports two core research directions: (1) elucidating molecular mechanisms of plant cell dedifferentiation and dynamic gene expressing during callus development, and (2) comparing totipotency-related transcriptional profiles between wild and cultivated carrot subspecies. sec.title: Sample collection
sec.p: Four carrot accessions with different differentiation ability were sourced from the Institute of Vegetables and Flowers, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, including three local cultivated carrot (C815, C819, and C824) and one wild carrot Ws. The sterilized seeds of the four materials were inoculated on MS basal medium for 10 days to obtain sterile seedlings. Hypocotyls were excised for subsequent culture and RNA sample extraction. For callus induction (0–20 days after culture), hypocotyl explants from the four materials were cultured on MS basal medium supplemented with 1 mg/L 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D) and 1 mg/L 6-benzyladenine (6-BA). For shoot regeneration (20–70 days), induced calli were transferred to hormone-free MS basal medium. All cultures were maintained at 26°C under a 16 h light / 8 h dark photoperiod. Tissue samples were collected at 0, 20, 70, and 120 days after hypocotyl culture initiation. At each time point, three entire cultured tissues from a single Petri dish as one biological replicate, including callus and early differentiated structures, and three independent Petri dishes were used to generate three biological replicates. All samples were ground to a fine powder in liquid nitrogen and stored at –80°C for subsequent RNA extraction. Total RNA was isolated using Tri-RNA Reagent. To ensure high-quality input for transcriptome sequencing, RNA concentration was measured with a Qubit 4.0 Fluorometer/MD microplate reader, and integrity was precisely detected using a Qsep400 Bioanalyzer [4].

sec.title: Library construction and sequencing data generation
sec.p: After passing quality inspection, RNA samples were processed by first isolating mRNA, synthesizing cDNA, and then completing the entire library preparation through steps including end repair, A-tailing, adapter ligation, purification, PCR amplification, denaturation, and circularization. After library construction, quality control was performed as follows prior to sequencing: (1) preliminary quantification using Qubit 2.0 and detection of insert size using Agilent 2100; sequencing proceeded only if the insert size met expectations; (2) accurate quantification of effective library concentration via Q-PCR (library effective concentration >2 nM).

sec.title: Sequencing
sec.p: After the library passed quality control, DNA Nano Ball (DNB) preparation was carried out: the linearized library fragments were placed in an optimized reaction system for rolling-circle amplification (RCA), generating single-stranded hyper-branched DNBs. Subsequently, via DNA nanoball hybridization technology, the DNBs were uniformly anchored to specific sites on the patterned sequencing chip, after loading the chip into the high-throughput sequencer, sequencing was completed in accordance with the instrument’s standard operating procedures, and raw sequencing reads were finally obtained [5].

sec.title: Read alignment to reference genome
sec.p: Perform strict quality control on the raw sequencing reads with the fastp tool [6]. Reads containing sequencing adapters were removed; reads with an N-base content exceeding 10% were filtered out; and reads with a low-quality base (Q ≤ 20) content greater than 50% were discarded, yielding high-quality clean reads. Based on the carrot reference genome DH1_v3.0[[7], [8]], an index was constructed using HISAT2 [9], and the clean reads were aligned to the reference genome.

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: High-quality clean reads were mapped to the carrot reference genome to obtain gene expression data. Principal component analysis (PCA) was then performed and visualized: each sample is represented by a scatter point, with different colors denoting distinct genotypes and culture periods. the axes represent Principal Component 1 (PC1), Principal Component 2 (PC2), and their respective contribution rates. Differential expression analysis between groups was conducted using DESeq2 v1.22.1 software with P-value correction. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were screened using the criteria of |log₂(fold change)| ≥ 1 and false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05. These DEGs were then visualized in a volcano plot, where the x-axis represents log₂(fold change) and the y-axis represents -log₁₀(FDR). In this plot, red and blue dots represent upregulated and downregulated DEGs, respectively, while grey dots represent non-differentially expressed genes.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: In terms of material selection, the tested carrot materials have limitations in their sources, failing to cover all carroy genotypes in this study. Consequently, the selected materials offer only limited representation of the spectrum of callus induction and differentiation capacities.
